transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

On a Bosch SMS25AW00G, E:09 usually means a fault in the heating circuit. Given the dishes complete a cycle but are stone cold, that fits very well: it is washing/pumping, but not heating the water or drying properly.

Most commonly this is:

• Failed heater / heat-pump assembly (the heater is often integrated into the circulation pump on Bosch models)
• Less commonly, a wiring/connector issue
• Occasionally a fault on the control board (heater relay/drive circuit)

### Is it expensive?
Potentially moderately expensive rather than a cheap reset-type repair.

Typical UK ballpark costs:

| Repair | Approx. fitted cost |
|---|---:|
| Diagnosis / call-out | £80–£130 |
| Wiring/connection repair | £120–£220 |
| Heater/heat-pump replacement | £220–£400 |
| Control board replacement | £250–£450+ |

A Bosch-authorised repair can be toward the higher end, particularly if both the pump/heater and electronics are implicated.

### Is it worth repairing?
The SMS25AW00G is likely an older machine, so it depends on its general condition. If the quote is around £250–£300, repair can make sense if it has otherwise been reliable and is in good condition. Once a quote approaches £400+, it is worth comparing against a replacement dishwasher, especially if it is around 8–12 years old.

### What to do now
• Turn it off at the mains / unplug it if possible.
• A power reset may clear the displayed error temporarily, but it will not normally cure E:09 if the heater has failed.
• Book an engineer and describe it as: “Bosch dishwasher E:09, completes washes but no heat.” That should save diagnostic time.
• Avoid repeatedly running it; cold cycles are unlikely to clean hygienically and repeated attempts will not fix the underlying heater fault.

If you can provide the appliance’s approximate age and whether it is integrated or freestanding, I can give a better view of whether the likely repair cost is worthwhile.
It's freestanding and 9 years old. Is there anything I can check myself first? I have a multimeter, though I'm not very confident with the wiring.

Yes — there are a few sensible checks, but avoid any live electrical testing. Since the dishwasher runs normally but never heats, the likely fault remains the heater element within the circulation/heat-pump unit.

## Before opening it

1. Switch off at the socket and unplug it.
2. Turn off the water supply and pull the machine out.
3. Remove the lower basket, filters and any standing water from the sump.
4. Leave it unplugged for 10–15 minutes before touching anything electrical.

A fuse or wall-socket problem is very unlikely, since the dishwasher can still run a wash cycle.

## The useful multimeter check: heater resistance

On this Bosch generation, the heater is normally built into the circulation pump / heat-pump assembly underneath the dishwasher. Access usually involves removing a side panel and/or the bottom tray. The exact layout can vary by the full E-Nr (model number) — usually on the top or side edge of the dishwasher door.

You are looking for the heater’s two heavier-gauge supply wires going to the circulation pump assembly, usually underneath.

### What to inspect first
With it unplugged:

• Look for a loose plug, green corrosion, overheated/browned plastic, or burnt terminals around the pump/heater connector.
• Check that the cable harness has not been rubbed through or trapped.
• Take photos before unplugging anything.

A damaged connector or wire can occasionally be a relatively inexpensive repair.

### Measuring the element
1. Disconnect the heater’s electrical connector from the pump — do not measure through the dishwasher wiring or circuit board.
2. Put the meter on resistance/ohms (`Ω`), ideally the lowest suitable range.
3. Put one probe on each of the two heater terminals.

For a roughly 2 kW heater on UK 230 V electricity, you would expect approximately:

20–30 Ω — broadly plausible / element probably has continuity.

Results suggesting a failed heater:

• OL / open circuit / infinite resistance: heater element has failed.
• Very high resistance (hundreds or thousands of ohms): likely failed.
• Near 0 Ω: short circuit fault; do not reconnect or run it.

You can also check each heater terminal to the metal body/earth of the pump:

• One probe on a heater terminal, the other on clean bare metal of the pump/chassis.
• Repeat for the other terminal.

A normal basic multimeter should show OL / no continuity. Any low resistance or continuity to earth is suspicious. Note, however, that a standard multimeter cannot perform a proper insulation-resistance test; an engineer would use a megger for that.

## What the results mean

| Finding | Likely implication |
|---|---|
| Heater reads OL/open circuit | Heat-pump/heater assembly probably needs replacing |
| Heater about 20–30 Ω, connector burnt/loose | Wiring or connector repair may solve it |
| Heater about 20–30 Ω, wiring looks good | Could be control board, temperature sensing, or a heater fault that needs professional testing |
| Heater shorted to metal/earth | Do not use it; likely pump/heater replacement |

## Things not to do

• Do not try to bypass the heater, thermal protection, or wiring.
• Do not test heater voltage with the machine powered unless you are experienced working safely with mains appliances.
• Do not run it on its side or with panels removed.
• Be cautious tipping it: residual water can run into the base tray and create an additional fault/error.

At nine years old, if you confirm an open-circuit heater, it is likely a £200–£400 fitted repair. A DIY heat-pump replacement can cost less in parts, but it is a fairly involved job involving water hoses, clamps, seals and the base of the machine — not ideal as a first appliance repair. If it turns out to be only a burnt connector or damaged loom, it could be considerably cheaper.

Ok, I unplugged it, took the panel off and checked across the two heater terminals on the pump. The meter shows open circuit. Does that mean the heater has definitely gone, and is it worth fixing on a 9 year old machine?

An open-circuit (`OL`, `1`, or infinity) reading directly across the two disconnected heater terminals is very strong evidence that the heater element has failed. Combined with E:09 and completely cold washes, it is effectively the expected diagnosis.

It is not likely to be a sensor, wiring fault, or control-board fault if you genuinely measured directly on the two heater terminals with the connector removed: those faults would not make the heater itself read open circuit.

A normal reading would typically be around 20–30 Ω. Open circuit means the internal heating element has broken.

## What the repair normally involves

On this Bosch, the heater is generally part of the circulation pump / heat-pump assembly, rather than a separate inexpensive element. The unit is replaced as an assembly.

Typical UK costs:

• Parts only: roughly £100–£200, depending on the exact part and supplier
• Independent engineer, supplied and fitted: commonly £220–£350
• Bosch-authorised repair: often around £300–£450

The exact pump version must be matched using the full E-Nr and FD number from the rating plate on the door edge.

## Is it worth it at 9 years old?

My practical view:

• DIY repair: usually worth considering if the correct pump is nearer £100–£150 and the machine is otherwise sound — no leaks, noisy bearings, corrosion, rack damage, or recurring errors.
• Professional repair under about £250–£300: reasonable, particularly if you prefer avoiding replacement and the machine has been reliable.
• Quote of £350–£400 or more: I would normally replace a nine-year-old dishwasher instead.

A new equivalent freestanding Bosch dishwasher is likely to cost significantly more than a repair, but it will come with warranty, may use less energy/water, and avoids the possibility of another age-related failure soon after the pump repair.

## Important if considering DIY

Replacing the pump/heater typically means working from underneath, disconnecting hoses and clamps, dealing with residual water, and ensuring every seal and connector is refitted correctly. A leak into the base can trigger further faults or damage flooring. If you are not confident around wiring, it is a job where an independent appliance engineer is often the better value.

Do not reconnect or run the machine with exposed panels/connectors.
